questions.stem: Equilibrium price in a market is the price at which

options.text: the producer earns the highest possible profit
the consumer pays the lowest possible amount
government has fixed the price by law

questions.explanation: Equilibrium simply means balance: buyers want exactly the quantity sellers are offering, so there is no unsatisfied buyer and no unsold stock to push the price either way.

distractorRationale.b: Maximum profit is the firm's objective, and it need not occur at the market-clearing price for the industry
distractorRationale.c: The lowest price consumers would like would leave a large shortage
distractorRationale.d: A legally fixed price is a controlled price, which is normally different from equilibrium

questions.stem: In a market for beans the schedule is: ₦100 — demand 80, supply 20; ₦200 — demand 60, supply 40; ₦300 — demand 50, supply 50; ₦400 — demand 40, supply 62. What is the equilibrium price in naira? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: Equilibrium occurs where the two quantities are equal. At ₦300 both demand and supply are 50 bags, so ₦300 clears the market and 50 bags is the equilibrium quantity.

questions.stem: Using the same beans schedule (₦200 — demand 60, supply 40), government fixes a maximum price of ₦200 per bag. The immediate result is

options.text: no change in the market at all

questions.explanation: A maximum price below equilibrium keeps the price artificially low, so demand of 60 exceeds supply of 40 and 20 bags of demand go unsatisfied. That gap is what drives queues, hoarding and black market trading.

distractorRationale.a: Surpluses follow minimum prices set above equilibrium, not ceilings
distractorRationale.c: 100 is the sum of the two quantities rather than the difference between them
distractorRationale.d: A ceiling below equilibrium always bites; only a ceiling above equilibrium would be ineffective

questions.stem: If demand for cement increases while supply remains unchanged, the equilibrium
questions.explanation: A rightward shift of demand creates excess demand at the old price. As buyers bid the price up, producers extend supply along the unchanged supply curve, so the new equilibrium has both a higher price and a larger quantity traded.

distractorRationale.b: Quantity falls only when supply decreases, which has not happened here
distractorRationale.c: A falling price with a rising quantity is the result of an increase in supply
distractorRationale.d: Both falling is the result of a decrease in demand

questions.stem: A bumper harvest of tomatoes, with demand unchanged, will cause the equilibrium price to

options.text: rise, and the quantity traded to fall
fall, and the quantity traded to rise
rise, and the quantity traded to rise
remain the same, since demand has not changed

questions.explanation: A bumper harvest shifts supply to the right, creating excess supply at the old price. Sellers cut prices to clear the crop, and the lower price extends demand, so more tomatoes change hands at a lower price.

distractorRationale.a: That is the effect of a fall in supply, such as after flooding
distractorRationale.c: Price and quantity both rising indicates an increase in demand
distractorRationale.d: Equilibrium responds to a shift in either curve, not only to demand

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely consequence of a minimum price fixed above the equilibrium price?

options.text: A shortage that encourages black market trading
A surplus that government may have to buy into a buffer stock
An immediate fall in the cost of production
A rightward shift of the demand curve

questions.explanation: Holding the price above equilibrium encourages producers to supply more while discouraging buyers, so unsold output accumulates. Governments usually mop this up through buffer stock purchases or restrain it with production quotas.

distractorRationale.a: Shortages and black markets follow maximum prices set below equilibrium
distractorRationale.c: A price floor changes the price received, not the technology or input costs of production
distractorRationale.d: A higher enforced price contracts demand along the existing curve; it does not shift the curve

questions.stem: A maximum price fixed above the equilibrium price will have no effect on the market.
questions.explanation: True. A ceiling only binds if it prevents the price from rising to equilibrium. Set above equilibrium, the market simply settles at the lower equilibrium price and the law is never triggered.

distractorRationale.b: This assumes every legal limit bites; a ceiling higher than the market price is legally present but economically idle

questions.stem: In a market where the ruling price is above equilibrium, the process that restores equilibrium is best described as

options.text: unsold stock forcing sellers to cut price, which extends demand and contracts supply
disappointed buyers bidding the price up until supply expands
government stepping in to fix a new legal price
the demand curve shifting rightward until it meets supply

questions.explanation: Above equilibrium there is excess supply. Sellers competing to clear stock reduce the price, which draws in more buyers along the demand curve while making production less attractive along the supply curve, until the two quantities meet.

distractorRationale.b: Buyers bid price up only when there is excess demand, which happens below equilibrium
distractorRationale.c: Markets return to equilibrium without any government action; that is the point of the price mechanism
distractorRationale.d: The curves do not move; only the price and the quantities along them adjust

questions.stem: In a market for rice, if the equilibrium price is ₦150 and the government sets a maximum price of ₦120, what is likely to occur?
questions.explanation: Setting a maximum price below the equilibrium price creates a situation where the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied, leading to a shortage. Consumers want to buy more rice at the lower price, but producers are not willing to supply enough at that price.

distractorRationale.a: A surplus occurs when the price is set above equilibrium, not below.
distractorRationale.c: Equilibrium cannot remain unchanged if a price control is imposed.
distractorRationale.d: Producers are less likely to supply more rice at a lower price.

questions.stem: What happens when there is excess supply in a market?
questions.explanation: Excess supply means that the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded at the current price. To eliminate this surplus, sellers will lower their prices, which in turn increases demand and helps restore equilibrium.

distractorRationale.a: Prices rise only when there is excess demand, not excess supply.
distractorRationale.c: Equilibrium is not established until the surplus is eliminated.
distractorRationale.d: Demand does not increase solely due to excess supply.

questions.stem: If the government imposes a minimum price for sugar that is below the equilibrium price, what will be the effect?
questions.explanation: A minimum price set below the equilibrium price will have no effect on the market because the market price will naturally remain above the minimum price. Thus, producers and consumers will continue to operate at the equilibrium price.

distractorRationale.b: A surplus occurs only when the minimum price is set above the equilibrium price.
distractorRationale.c: A shortage arises when the maximum price is below equilibrium, not a minimum price.
distractorRationale.d: Consumer demand will not necessarily increase due to a minimum price set below equilibrium.

questions.stem: In the context of market equilibrium, what does the term 'price elasticity of demand' refer to?

options.text: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price
The relationship between supply and demand
The fixed price in a market
The total revenue generated from sales

questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand measures how much the quantity demanded of a good responds to changes in its price. A higher elasticity indicates that consumers are more sensitive to price changes.

distractorRationale.b: While it relates to supply and demand, elasticity specifically refers to demand response to price changes.
distractorRationale.c: The fixed price does not define elasticity; elasticity measures responsiveness.
distractorRationale.d: Total revenue is influenced by elasticity but is not the definition of price elasticity.

questions.stem: What is the primary effect of a maximum price control on a product?
questions.explanation: A maximum price control typically leads to a shortage because it sets the price below the equilibrium level, resulting in higher demand than supply. Producers may not find it profitable to produce enough of the product at this lower price.

distractorRationale.a: Production may decrease as suppliers are discouraged by lower prices.
distractorRationale.c: Consumer choice may decrease due to the shortage of goods.
distractorRationale.d: Quality may suffer as producers cut costs to maintain profitability.

questions.stem: What is the likely outcome if a government sets a minimum price at which a good must be sold?
questions.explanation: When a minimum price is set above the equilibrium price, it creates a surplus because the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded at that price. Producers are willing to supply more, but consumers are not willing to buy as much.

distractorRationale.b: Equilibrium price does not decrease due to a minimum price; it may increase.
distractorRationale.c: A shortage occurs only when a maximum price is set below equilibrium.
distractorRationale.d: Demand does not necessarily increase; it may actually decrease due to higher prices.

questions.stem: If the demand for a product increases while supply remains constant, what happens to the equilibrium price?
questions.explanation: An increase in demand, with supply held constant, leads to a higher equilibrium price. As consumers are willing to pay more for the same quantity of goods, prices will rise until a new equilibrium is reached.

distractorRationale.a: The price does not decrease; it increases with higher demand.
distractorRationale.b: Equilibrium cannot remain unchanged with a shift in demand.
distractorRationale.d: Fluctuations are not typical; the price moves to a new equilibrium.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes 'market equilibrium'?

options.text: When quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
When prices are fixed by the government

questions.explanation: Market equilibrium occurs when the quantity demanded by consumers is equal to the quantity supplied by producers at a certain price level. This balance ensures that there is neither surplus nor shortage in the market.

distractorRationale.a: This describes a state of excess demand, not equilibrium.
distractorRationale.b: This describes excess supply, which is the opposite of equilibrium.
distractorRationale.d: Government price fixing does not define market equilibrium; it can disrupt it.

questions.stem: How does a price ceiling affect consumer behavior?

options.text: Has no effect on purchasing decisions

questions.explanation: A price ceiling, which is a maximum price set below equilibrium, typically encourages more purchasing as consumers find the lower price attractive. However, this can lead to shortages as suppliers may not produce enough to meet the increased demand.

distractorRationale.b: Consumers are generally encouraged to purchase more at lower prices.
distractorRationale.c: Price ceilings directly impact purchasing decisions by altering the cost of goods.
distractorRationale.d: Quality is not necessarily increased; it may even decline due to lower prices.

questions.stem: Which of the following scenarios illustrates a surplus in the market?

options.text: Supply exceeds demand at a certain price

questions.explanation: A surplus occurs when the quantity supplied of a good exceeds the quantity demanded at a specific price. This often happens when prices are set too high, leading to excess supply.

distractorRationale.a: A maximum price usually leads to a shortage, not a surplus.
distractorRationale.b: This scenario would likely lead to a shortage, not a surplus.
distractorRationale.d: Establishing equilibrium does not create a surplus; it balances supply and demand.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the term 'shortage' in a market?
questions.explanation: A shortage occurs when the quantity demanded for a product is greater than the quantity supplied at a specific price. This situation often arises when prices are set too low, leading to increased demand and insufficient supply.

distractorRationale.a: This describes a surplus, which is the opposite of a shortage.
distractorRationale.c: Equilibrium price is not maintained during a shortage; it may rise.
distractorRationale.d: While producers may be unwilling to supply at low prices, the key factor is the imbalance between demand and supply.

questions.stem: In a competitive market, when there is excess demand, what is likely to happen to the price?
questions.explanation: Excess demand occurs when consumers want to purchase more of a good than is available at the current price. This leads to upward pressure on prices as consumers compete to buy the limited supply, pushing the price higher until equilibrium is restored.

distractorRationale.a: This option is incorrect because excess demand typically leads to an increase in price, not a decrease.
distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect as prices do not remain the same when there is excess demand; they adjust to restore equilibrium.
distractorRationale.d: This option is misleading since prices generally trend in one direction rather than fluctuating wildly.

options.text: It has no effect on the market.

questions.explanation: A price floor set below the equilibrium price does not affect the market because the market price will naturally rise to the equilibrium level. Therefore, the price floor is ineffective and has no impact on supply or demand.

distractorRationale.b: This option is incorrect because a price floor below equilibrium does not lead to a surplus; it is ineffective.
distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect as a price floor below equilibrium does not create a shortage; it simply does not change the market situation.
distractorRationale.d: This option is incorrect because a price floor below equilibrium does not stabilize prices; it is irrelevant.

distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect as the market will not remain unchanged; the maximum price will create an imbalance.

questions.stem: How does an increase in supply affect the equilibrium price, assuming demand remains constant?

options.text: It has no effect on the equilibrium price.

questions.explanation: An increase in supply, with demand held constant, leads to a surplus of goods at the original price. To eliminate this surplus, the price must decrease, which will eventually lead to a new equilibrium at a lower price.

distractorRationale.a: This option is incorrect because an increase in supply does not raise the equilibrium price; it lowers it.
distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect as an increase in supply will definitely affect the equilibrium price.
distractorRationale.d: This option is incorrect because while a surplus may occur initially, the price will adjust downward to eliminate it.

questions.explanation: Excess supply occurs when the quantity supplied of a good exceeds the quantity demanded at a given price. This situation typically leads to downward pressure on prices as suppliers attempt to sell off their surplus inventory.

distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect as stable prices do not necessarily indicate excess supply.

questions.stem: When the government imposes a price control, what is the primary goal?

options.text: To protect consumers from high prices.
To ensure producers make maximum profit.

questions.explanation: The primary goal of government-imposed price controls, such as price ceilings, is to protect consumers from excessively high prices, making essential goods more affordable. This is particularly important during times of crisis or inflation.

distractorRationale.a: This option is incorrect as price controls do not inherently increase competition; they can sometimes reduce it.
distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect because while price controls may address some surpluses, they do not eliminate all of them.
distractorRationale.d: This option is incorrect as price controls often limit producer profits in order to protect consumers.
